bib.title: Reaching Agreement Among Reasoning LLM Agents

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Reaching Agreement Among Reasoning LLM Agents", Chaoyi Ruan, Yiliang Wang, Ziji Shi, Jialin Li (NUS). arXiv:2512.20184v1 [cs.DC], 23 Dec 2025. Preprint; the text shows no venue.
COVERAGE: 73,881 of 73,881 chars read, covering every page and the references. There is no appendix and no limitations section. The figures are plots, so I read their captions and the text that describes them, not the plotted values.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Simple majority voting across refinement rounds is unstable. Agents revise their answers after seeing peer reasoning, so a majority can flip between rounds. A fixed round limit or "stop at majority" rule can therefore commit a transient state.
  number: none (the example is 3 agents, (17,17,13) then (13,17,13)).
  setup: a conceptual example (Fig 3), backed by the Table 2 flip counts below.
  quote: "A solution supported by majority agents in a round may dissolve in the next round as agents refine their positions after considering peer rationales."
  where: p2, Sec 1; Fig 3 on p3
- Aegean is a leader-based, Raft-like consensus protocol for stochastic agents. It finalizes an answer only when at least α agents agree (the quorum) and that answer has persisted for β consecutive rounds (the stability horizon). A candidate that is overturned resets the stability counter to 1.
  number: defaults n=3, α=2, β=2, Tmax=5.
  setup: Sec 5, Fig 5 (fast path and slow path). Equivalence between answers is judged by exact match, embedding similarity or LLM-as-judge.
  quote: "Unless otherwise specified, Aegean uses default parameters: n=3 agents, α=2 (majority quorum size), β=2 rounds (stability horizon threshold),T max=5 rounds."
  where: p10, Sec 7.1; p7
- Safety and liveness are proved: refinement validity, refinement monotonicity and refinement termination.
  number: none.
  setup: the proofs rest on Assumption 1 (an agent given a set of solutions can match the best one), which the authors do not prove for LLMs. They assume at most ⌈(N−1)/2⌉ fail-stop agents and a partially synchronous network.
  quote: "Given the stochastic nature of existing AI models, proving formal guarantees of an agent is outside the scope of this work."
  where: p5, Sec 4.2
- Latency drops by 1.2–20× against the Multi-Agent-Base baseline, with accuracy within 2.5%. The baseline is barrier-synchronized with fixed round limits and majority voting.
  number: 1.2–20× average latency, up to 11× P99.
  setup: 5 local open models on 8×H100 with vLLM 0.10 (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, GPT-OSS-20B, Mistral-7B, DeepSeek-Qwen-2.5-7B). Benchmarks are GSM8K, MMLU, AIME and IMO, with Poisson arrivals at 0.1–1.0 req/s. The 20× figure is AIME at 1.0 req/s against MaxRound=6.
  quote: "On AIME at 1.0 requests/sec, MaxRound=4/5/6 reach 937s, 2662s, and 6571s (2.9×, 8.2×, and 20.2× higher)"
  where: p10, Sec 7.2
- The speedups hold for commercial APIs at 0.5 req/s (GPT-5-mini, Claude-4.5-Haiku, Gemini-2.5-Flash via OpenRouter).
  number: 6.2× on GSM8K, 4.1× on MMLU, 2.7× on AIME, 2.7× on IMO.
  quote: "8.0s vs 49.2s on GSM8K (6.2× speedup), 13.8s vs 57.2s on MMLU (4.1× speedup), 26.4s vs 72.5s on AIME (2.7× speedup) and 198.8s vs 543.6s on IMO (2.7× speedup)."
  where: p11
- Accuracy: Aegean is slightly below Multi-Agent-Base and well above the best single model.
  number: GSM8K 97 vs 98 vs 93 (best single). AIME 60 for both multi-agent systems vs 46.7. IMO 47 (Aegean) vs 49.5 (Multi-Agent-Base) vs 18.
  setup: heterogeneous ensemble; the text does not say which single model is best. The AIME set is AIME-2024. The paper gives no variance, seeds or sample counts for these runs.
  quote: "IMO exhibits the largest gap: Multi-Agent-Base reaches 49.5% and Aegean achieves 47%, compared to only 18% for the best single model."
  where: p11
- Fixed round limits misalign cost with difficulty, and barriers couple latency to stragglers.
  number: average rounds to converge are 2.0 (GSM8K), 2.3 (MMLU) and 4.1 (AIME). The slowest model is 11×, 18× and 64× slower than the fastest. On GSM8K the slowest model was DeepSeek-R1 in 50% of rounds, GPT-5-mini in 42% and Gemini in 8%.
  setup: Table 1, GPT-5-mini, Gemini-2.5-Flash and DeepSeek-R1.
  quote: "AIME exhibits the most severe disparity, where the slowest model takes 370.6s compared to the fastest at 5.8s, a 64 × difference."
  where: p3-4, Table 1 and Sec 3
- Stability horizon β: β=1 is premature termination, and β above 2 only adds time.
  number: GSM8K accuracy is 85% at β=1 and about 98% at β=2, 3 and 4. Time rises from 4.8s at β=1 to 9.7s at β=4.
  setup: 3 models, α=2, GSM8K only.
  quote: "At β=1 , accuracy drops to 85%, indicating premature termination before models reach true consensus."
  where: p12
- Quorum α: a majority is enough.
  number: IMO accuracy is about 43% at α=3, 4 and 5. Latency grows from 1346s to 1695s, and tokens from 127K to 143K. At α=1 latency is 17s with near-zero accuracy.
  setup: 5 open models, IMO, N=5.
  quote: "Stricter thresholds provide no accuracy benefit while imposing 17-26% additional latency overhead."
  where: p12
- Agent-semantics check: a weak model improves after seeing a strong model's traces, and a strong model barely changes after seeing weak traces.
  number: Llama-3.1-8B goes from 3% to 54.4% on AIME, 43% to 79% on MMLU and 88% to 96% on GSM8K. DeepSeek-R1 changes by 0 to +2 points, with decision flips of 1/100, 1/100 and 10/90.
  setup: pairwise exchange, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1, on AIME-Validation (90 problems), MMLU (100) and GSM8K (100).
  quote: "Accuracy increases from 3% to 54.4% on AIME-Validation (+51%), from 43% to 79% on MMLU (+36%), and from 88% to 96% on GSM8K (+8%)."
  where: p5, Table 2
- Token savings from early termination are largest on easy tasks.
  number: 4.4× on GSM8K (1.3K vs 5.7K tokens), 3.3× on MMLU, 1.3× on AIME, 1.1× on IMO.
  quote: "AIME shows 1.3× reduction (46.0K vs 59.9K tokens) and IMO shows 1.1× reduction (64.8K vs 73.8K tokens)."
  where: p13, Sec 7.4
- Ensemble scaling is sub-linear, using homogeneous Qwen3-8B replicas.
  number: going from 3 to 7 replicas costs +33% time on GSM8K, +23% on MMLU, +28% on AIME and +27% on IMO.
  quote: "AIME increases from 99.9s to 127.7s (28% overhead) and IMO grows from 188.8s to 240.4s (27% overhead)"
  where: p12

LIMITS
- No limitations section. Assumption 1 (reasoning refinement) is justified only by the small Table 2 experiment on two models.
- That experiment pairs one weak and one strong model. It does not test same-strength agents, correlated wrong majorities, or an adversarial or confidently wrong agent.
- The paper itself notes that "a majority of agents may incidentally arrive at the same wrong solution". Stability does not guard against this. Quality is bounded below only by the "majority optimal" solution, and the Quality Oracle Q is never implemented.
- The failure model is fail-stop only, so it covers neither Byzantine nor adversarial agents.
- Only math and MCQ reasoning benchmarks were tested. There is no open-ended, tool-use or code task.
- No error bars. The overall accuracy cost is "within 2.5%", and the baselines are the authors' own reimplementation of TUMIX-style systems, not the original systems.
- The paper does not use the phrase "consensus deadlock". It addresses non-termination only through Tmax=5 and leader change, and it does not report how often Tmax is hit.
- The multi-instance variant is omitted. Leader election and term change are specified, but no leader-failure experiment is reported.
- Some internal figures look inconsistent. The ensemble ablation says AIME accuracy peaks at 95.8% with homogeneous Qwen3-8B, against 60% in Fig 9. IMO accuracy at α=3 is about 43%, against 47% in Fig 9. Check the figure values before quoting these.

BUILDS ON
- Self-consistency (Wang et al., arXiv 2022).
- Multi-agent debate (Du et al., 2023).
- TUMIX (Chen et al., 2025).
- Mixture-of-Agents (Wang et al., ICLR 2025).
- MAGICORE (Chen et al., 2024).
- AutoGen (Wu et al., 2023).
- Paxos (Lamport) and Paxos Made Moderately Complex (Van Renesse and Altinbuken, ACM Computing Surveys 2015).
- Raft (Ongaro and Ousterhout; the reference text is in the truncated part).
- PBFT (Castro and Liskov, OSDI 1999).
- Partial synchrony (Dwork, Lynch and Stockmeyer, J. ACM 1988).
- vLLM (2025).
- Related serving systems: Parrot, Autellix, Kairos, Gradientsys.

CODE
The Aegean-Serve engine interface, p9, Sec 6.1:
def Dispatch(q: str, ctx: ConsensusCtx, eid: int) -> Handle
def OnComplete(h: Handle, cb: Callable[[Answer], None])
def Cancel(h: Handle) -> bool
def QueryEnsemble(eid: int) -> EnsembleState
Algorithm 1 (p6) is pseudocode of the round loop: broadcast RefmSet, collect a quorum of Refm, feed the decision engine.

FIGURES
Candidate: Fig 5, p7. "Aegean consensus execution examples with α=2 and β=2 among 3 agents. Three boxes in each round represent responses from three agents." It shows a fast path (13,13,17 stable for 2 rounds, so finalize) and a slow path where the 17 majority is overturned, the counter resets, and 13 finalizes in round 3. This is the quickest way to see stability-horizon termination. Fig 3 (p3, majority flip) is the alternative for the failure itself.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction was clean. Figure axes came out as numbers only.
- No embedded instructions found.
- The Raft reference entry fell in the truncated middle of the references and was not read.
